### 1966–1977 Red Data Lists

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1966–1977 Red Data Lists")]

Initially the Red Data Lists were designed for specialists and were issued in a loose-leaf format that could be easily changed.

The first two volumes of Red Lists were published in 1966 by conservationist Noel Simon, one for mammals and one for birds.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-9)

The third volume that appeared covered reptiles and amphibians. It was created by René E. Honegger in 1968.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-10)

In 1970, the IUCN published volume 5 in this series. This was the first Red Data List which focused on plants ([angiosperms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant "Flowering plant") only), compiled by [Ronald Melville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Melville_(botanist) "Ronald Melville (botanist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-11)

The final volume created in the loose leaf style was volume 4 on freshwater fishes. This was published in 1979 by [Robert Rush Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rush_Miller "Robert Rush Miller").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-12)

### 1969 Red Data Book

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1969 Red Data Book")]

The first attempt to create a Red Data Book for a nonspecialist public came in 1969 with _The Red Book: Wildlife in Danger_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-13) This book covered various groups but was predominantly about mammals and birds, with smaller sections on reptiles, amphibians, fishes, and plants.

### 2006 release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2006 release")]

The 2006 Red List, released on 4 May 2006 evaluated 40,168 species as a whole, plus an additional 2,160 [subspecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subspecies "Subspecies"), [varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_(botany) "Variety (botany)"), aquatic [stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_stocks "Fish stocks"), and [subpopulations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_population "Statistical population").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-14)

### 2007 release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2007 release")]

On 12 September 2007, the [World Conservation Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Conservation_Union "World Conservation Union") (IUCN) released the **2007 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species**. In this release, they have raised their classification of both the [western lowland gorilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_lowland_gorilla "Western lowland gorilla") (_Gorilla gorilla gorilla_) and the [Cross River gorilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_River_gorilla "Cross River gorilla") (_Gorilla gorilla diehli_) from [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered "Endangered") to [critically endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critically_endangered "Critically endangered"), which is the last category before extinct in the wild, due to [Ebola virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebola_virus "Ebola virus") and [poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poaching "Poaching"), along with other factors. [Russ Mittermeier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russ_Mittermeier "Russ Mittermeier"), chief of [Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland")-based IUCN's Primate Specialist Group, stated that 16,306 species are endangered with extinction, 188 more than in 2006 (total of 41,415 species on the Red List). The Red List includes the [Sumatran orangutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatran_orangutan "Sumatran orangutan") (_Pongo abelii_) in the Critically Endangered category and the [Bornean orangutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bornean_orangutan "Bornean orangutan") (_Pongo pygmaeus_) in the Endangered category.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-15)

### 2008 release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2008 release")]

The 2008 Blue List was released on 6 October 2008 at the IUCN World Conservation Congress in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") and "confirmed an extinction crisis, with almost one in four [mammals] at risk of disappearing forever". The study shows at least 1,141 of the 5,487 mammals on Earth are known to be threatened with extinction, and 836 are listed as [Data Deficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_Deficient "Data Deficient").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-16)

### 2012 release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2012 release")]

The Red List of 2012 was released 19 July 2012 at [Rio+20 Earth Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Conference_on_Sustainable_Development "United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development");[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-CNNrio-17) nearly 2,000 species were added,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-RedList2000-18) with 4 species to the extinct list, 2 to the rediscovered list.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-IUCN2012-19) The IUCN assessed a total of 63,837 species which revealed 19,817 are threatened with extinction.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-RedListReport-20) 3,947 were described as "critically endangered" and 5,766 as "endangered", while more than 10,000 species are listed as "vulnerable".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-21) At threat are 41% of amphibian species, 33% of reef-building corals, 30% of conifers, 25% of mammals, and 13% of birds.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-RedListReport-20) The IUCN Red List has listed 132 species of plants and animals from India as "Critically Endangered".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-IndiaRedList-22)

Species are classified by the IUCN Red List into nine groups,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-23) specified through criteria such as rate of decline, population size, area of geographic distribution, and degree of population and distribution fragmentation.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-Mace_1424%E2%80%931442-24) There is an emphasis on the acceptability of applying any criteria in the absence of high quality data including suspicion and potential future threats, "so long as these can reasonably be supported".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-25):6

*   [Extinct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinct "Extinct") (EX) – beyond reasonable doubt that the species is no longer extant.
*   Extinct in the wild (EW) – survives only in captivity, cultivation and/or outside native range, as presumed after exhaustive surveys.
*   [Critically endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critically_endangered "Critically endangered") (CR) – in a particularly and extremely critical state.
*   [Endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered "Endangered") (EN) – very high risk of extinction in the wild, meets any of criteria A to E for Endangered.
*   [Vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") (VU) – meets one of the 5 Red List criteria and thus considered to be at high risk of unnatural (human-caused) extinction without further human intervention.
*   [Near Threatened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_Threatened "Near Threatened") (NT) – close to being endangered in the near future.
*   [Least Concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_Concern "Least Concern") (LC) – widespread and abundant in the wild.
*   [Data Deficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_Deficient "Data Deficient") (DD) – inadequate information to assess extinction risk.
*   [Not Evaluated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_Evaluated "Not Evaluated") (NE) – has not yet been assessed.

In the IUCN Red List, "[threatened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threatened_species "Threatened species")" embraces the categories of Critically Endangered, Endangered, and Vulnerable.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-Mace_1424%E2%80%931442-24)

### 1994 categories and 2001 framework

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1994 categories and 2001 framework")]

The older 1994 list has only a single "Lower Risk" category which contained three subcategories:

*   [Conservation Dependent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Dependent "Conservation Dependent") (LR/cd)
*   [Near Threatened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_Threatened "Near Threatened") (LR/nt)
*   [Least Concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_Concern "Least Concern") (LR/lc)

In the 2001 framework, _Near Threatened_ and _Least Concern_ became their own categories, while _Conservation Dependent_ was removed and its contents merged into _Near Threatened_.

### Possibly extinct

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Possibly extinct")]

The tag of "possibly extinct" (PE)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-26) is used by [BirdLife International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BirdLife_International "BirdLife International"), the Red List Authority for birds for the IUCN Red List.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-27) BirdLife International has recommended PE become an official tag for Critically Endangered species, and this has now been adopted, along with a "Possibly Extinct in the Wild" tag for species with populations surviving in captivity but likely to be extinct in the wild.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-28)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=IUCN_Red_List&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Criticism")]

In 1997, the IUCN Red List received criticism on the grounds of secrecy (or at least poor documentation) surrounding the sources of its data.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-31) These allegations have led to efforts by the IUCN to improve its documentation and data quality, and to include peer reviews of taxa on the Red List.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-Mace_1424%E2%80%931442-24) The list is also open to petitions against its classifications, on the basis of documentation or criteria.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-32)

In the November 2002 issue of _[Trends in Ecology & Evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trends\_in\_Ecology\_&\_Evolution "Trends in Ecology & Evolution")_, an article suggested that the IUCN Red List and similar works are prone to misuse by governments and other groups that draw possibly inappropriate conclusions on the state of the environment or to affect [exploitation of natural resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploitation_of_natural_resources "Exploitation of natural resources").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-33)

In the November 2016 issue of _[Science Advances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_Advances "Science Advances")_, a research article claims there are serious inconsistencies in the way species are classified by the IUCN. The researchers contend that the IUCN's process of categorization is "out-dated, and leaves room for improvement", and further emphasize the importance of readily available and easy-to-include geospatial data, such as satellite and aerial imaging. Their conclusion questioned not only the IUCN's method but also the validity of where certain species fall on the List. They believe that combining geographical data can significantly increase the number of species that need to be reclassified to a higher risk category.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List#cite_note-Stocks_2016-34)

20 of the most endangered animals in North America

# 20 of the most endangered animals in North America

November 20, 2025

Want to help wildlife?[Join IFAW](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/20-most-endangered-animals-north-america?form=join)

In [Asia](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/18-of-the-most-endangered-animals-in-asia), [South America](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/16-most-endangered-animals-south-america), [Europe](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/most-endangered-species-europe), and beyond, wild animals are threatened by human activity. It’s no different in North America, where [more than one-third of US wildlife](https://www.livescience.com/more-than-a-third-of-us-wildlife-at-risk-of-extinction-grim-new-report-shows) is at risk of extinction.

Every animal—from the largest predator to the smallest insect—plays an essential part in its ecosystem. The loss of just one species has a significant impact on countless others. That’s why, at IFAW, we’re working to protect animals in North America and around the world. From [marine conservation](https://www.ifaw.org/programs/marine-conservation) to [disaster response](https://www.ifaw.org/programs/disaster-response) to raising public awareness of the threats animals face, we’re building a future where animals and people can thrive together.

Here, we look at the 20 most endangered animals in North America and the unique threats that each species faces.

##### **Red wolf**

![Image 1: Red wolf.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4062/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_503024760_441363_reduced.webp)

Red wolf. 

[Red wolves](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population) (_Canis rufus)_ are part of the dog family. They’re smaller than [grey wolves](http://ifaw.org/animals/wolves) but bigger than coyotes. As their name suggests, red wolves have tawny, red-grey coats.

Red wolves used to live throughout the eastern and southern US. They now live solely in North Carolina. They can thrive in various habitats, including forests, swamps, and coastal prairies, where they hunt white-tailed deer, raccoons, rabbits, and other small mammals.

Red wolves were declared extinct in the wild in [1980](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#assessment-information) but were reintroduced to North Carolina in [1987](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#assessment-information). The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) now categorizes red wolves as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population).

As of 2025, their population is still decreasing, with just [20 to 30 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population) left in the wild.

Red wolves face several threats, including hybridization with coyotes. Illegal killing of red wolves also continues, particularly when wolves come into conflict with landowners.

At IFAW, we’re [campaigning to end the practice of poisoning predators](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/predator-protection-canada) like wolves in Canada. We’re also working with local communities to promote peaceful [coexistence with wolves](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/predator-coexistence-united-states) and the use of non-lethal methods to reduce [human-wildlife conflicts](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/what-is-human-wildlife-conflict).

##### **Axolotl**

The [axolotl](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/1095/53947343) (_Ambystoma mexicanum_) is a unique-looking amphibian creature with feathery gills, webbed feet, a dorsal fin, and a mouth curved upwards into a permanent smile.

Axolotls are salamanders that never grow out of the larval phase. Instead, they continue to live in water and, unlike other amphibians, never make the transition to land.

Axolotls grow to be just [25 centimeters (10 inches)](https://www.britannica.com/animal/axolotl) long. They eat crustaceans, insect eggs, mollusks, and small fish. In the wild, their coloring is mostly grey-brown.

This animal is only found in Lake Xochimilco, a water system made up of canals, small lakes, and wetlands in Mexico City.

In 2025, the IUCN categorizes axolotls as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/1095/53947343), with a decreasing population. Despite improvements in recent years, pollution and draining of their habitat (to reduce flood risk) continue to threaten their survival.

##### **North Atlantic right whale**

![Image 2: North Atlantic right whale Horton (Catalog #3360) and the second calf of the 2023-4 calving season](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4818/image/p1300x1300/MC202312_NARWSecondCalf_002_459613_reduced.webp)

North Atlantic right whale Horton (Catalog #3360) and the second calf of the 2023-4 calving season, sighted December 07, 2023 approximately 22.2mi east of St. Catherine’s Island, GA. Photo: © Clearwater Marine Aquarium Research Institute, taken under NOAA permit #26919. Funded by United States Army Corps of Engineers

[The North Atlantic right whale](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/north-atlantic-right-whale) (_Eubalaena glacialis_) is a huge, slow-swimming baleen whale. It can grow up to [15 meters](https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/species-guide/north-atlantic-right-whale/) (49 feet) long and weigh [70,000 kilograms](https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/species-guide/north-atlantic-right-whale/)(154,000 pounds).

These whales live in the Atlantic Ocean, swimming in deep waters when searching for food and moving to shallower areas when calving. They feed on zooplankton, krill, and other small crustaceans.

The IUCN classes North Atlantic right whales as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/41712/178589687). As of 2025, only around [370 North Atlantic right whales](https://www.ifaw.org/press-releases/north-atlantic-right-whales-number-urgency) are left, with just [70 reproductive-age females](https://www.ifaw.org/campaigns/north-atlantic-right-whale-calving-season).

Key threats to North Atlantic right whales include [vessel strikes](https://www.ifaw.org/resources/ship-strikes-whales-prevention-factsheet) and entanglement in fishing gear. Whales are coming into contact with humans and fishing activity more regularly because climate change has shifted their usual habitats, increasing the danger members of the species face.

At IFAW, we’re working hard to [ensure the survival of the North Atlantic right whale](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/saving-the-north-atlantic-right-whale), by advocating for solutions to their biggest threats, vessel strikes and entanglement. Help us save this species by adding your name to our petition.

[Sign the petition](http://action.ifaw.org/page/125066/action/1)

##### **Bolson tortoise**

The [Bolson tortoise](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985) (_Gopherus flavomarginatus_) is the world’s [largest land reptile](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus). It can grow to [40 centimeters (5.75 inches)](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus), with females growing larger than males. The Bolson tortoise lives in a small area of grassland in Mexico and grazes on grasses and other plants.

This species of tortoise spends most of its time in an underground burrow that it digs with its front feet. These burrows are around [2.5 meters (8 feet) deep](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus) and [10 meters (32 feet) long](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus) and help protect the tortoises from predators and extreme temperatures.

The IUCN lists the Bolson tortoise as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985). As of 2025, there are around [2,500 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985) left, and their population is decreasing. Habitat degradation and overgrazing by cattle impact the grassland habitat where the Bolson tortoise lives, further threatening this species.

##### **Mojave Desert tortoise**

The [Mojave Desert tortoise](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/97246272/3150871#population) (_Gopherus agassizii_) has survived in the Mojave Desert for [millions of years](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/desert-tortoises). These medium-sized tortoises measure [23 to 28 centimeters](https://www.ifaw.org/au/animals/desert-tortoises) (9 to 15 inches) and weigh [3.5 to 7 kilograms](https://www.ifaw.org/au/animals/desert-tortoises)(8 to 15 pounds) as adults.

Mojave Desert tortoises are herbivores that feed on grasses, wildflowers, herbs, shrubs, and even cacti. They spend much of the year in hibernation, retreating to underground burrows to avoid the extreme temperatures of the desert.

The IUCN lists the Mojave Desert tortoise as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/97246272/3150871#population). Their population is severely fragmented, and adult numbers decreased by[36%](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2024-10/usfws_dtmonitoringupdate_mog_20241003_mitchell.pdf) between 2001 and 2020.

Human activity is largely to blame for the decline of the Mojave Desert tortoise. Towns, cities, and roads are breaking up and encroaching on the tortoise’s desert habitat. Additionally, invasive grasses are outcompeting the native plants that the Mojave Desert tortoise likes to eat, threatening their food sources.

##### **Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle**

![Image 3: After stranding in Cape Cod and undergoing four months of rehabilitation, a Kemp's ridley turtle is returned to the wild in New Smyrna Beach, Florida.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4819/image/p1300x1300/DSC_0063-2_edited.webp)

After stranding in Cape Cod and undergoing four months of rehabilitation, a Kemp's ridley turtle is returned to the wild in New Smyrna Beach, Florida. Photo: © IFAW

[Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/11533/155057916) (_Lepidochelys kempii_) is the world’s smallest sea turtle. Their shells typically measure up to [60 centimeters (2 feet)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle) in diameter and weigh up to [45 kilograms (100 pounds)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle). They can live to be [50 years old](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle).

In North America, most of these [sea turtles](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/sea-turtles) live in the Gulf of Mexico, but you can find them as far north as Nova Scotia.

Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles are migratory and can travel hundreds of miles when it’s time to lay their eggs. Females travel to the same beach where they hatched decades ago. There, they participate in a nesting procession called an [arribada](https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/reptiles/kemps-ridley-nesting-arribada). They drag their bodies across the beach in large groups, searching for the perfect place to lay their eggs.

The IUCN lists Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/11533/155057916). The biggest threat to their survival is fishing activity. The turtles get accidentally caught by fishing boats, which can lead to drowning or fatal injuries.

[Sign our petitions to protect animals](https://www.ifaw.org/take-action)

##### **Rice’s whale**

[Rice’s whale](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) (_Balaenoptera ricei_) lives in the Gulf of Mexico. They can grow up to [12.5 meters (41 feet)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) long and weigh up to [27,200 kilograms (60,000 pounds)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale).

These baleen whales dive to the bottom of the sea during the day and spend the night within [15 meters (50 feet)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) of the surface.

The IUCN lists Rice’s whale as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244). As of 2025, there are only [26 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) left, and their population is decreasing, making this [one of the most endangered whales](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) in the world.

These whales are most at risk from vessel strikes and entanglement in fishing gear. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill affected Rice’s whale habitat, too. Around [48% of the population](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) was exposed to oil, causing reproductive failure and ill health.

IFAW is campaigning for [reduced vessel speeds](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/protection-whales-climate-change-ship-speed-reduction), which would decrease the risk of [collisions](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/21st-century-shipping) and reduce [ocean noise pollution](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/ocean-noise-reduction-global). We’re also supporting the development of ropeless [fishing gear](https://www.ifaw.org/people/opinions/new-fishing-gear-crucial-saving-whales) to prevent entanglements.

##### **Hot Creek toad**

The [Hot Creek toad](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/181491536/182617236) (_Anaxyrus monfontanus_) is a toad species that was [only discovered in 2017](https://www.unr.edu/nevada-today/news/2017/new-toad-species-discovered). It has olive-grey coloring and lives in Nevada’s Great Basin in the Hot Creek Mountain Range. This area of marshy habitat is fed by hot springs and surrounded by a high-altitude desert, which may help to explain why these toads are confined to such a small and remote habitat.

Because we haven’t known about the Hot Creek toad for long, we don’t know much about its behavior or what conditions it needs for survival. The number of Hot Creek toads in the wild is also unknown, but the IUCN categorizes the species as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/181491536/182617236).

##### **Vancouver Island marmot**

![Image 4: Two Vancouver Island marmots on a rock.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4065/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_212902763_441366_reduced.webp)

Two Vancouver Island marmots on a rock. 

The [Vancouver Island marmot](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184) (_Marmota vancouverensis_) lives in the forest, grassland, and rocky mountain habitat of Canada’s Vancouver Island.

They are dark brown with white patches on their noses, their bellies, and the tops of their heads. They have brown, bushy tails.

This species is quite large compared to other marmots and rodents. They tend to be around [62 to 72 centimeters](https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/endangered-species/vancouver-island-marmot/) (just over 2 feet) long and weigh [3.5 to 5.5 kilograms](https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/endangered-species/vancouver-island-marmot/) (7-12 pounds). They lose weight during winter hibernation and put it back on in the spring and summer.

The IUCN categorizes the Vancouver Island marmot as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184). As of 2025, there are just [90 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184) left in the wild.

These marmots are particularly at risk from predators like cougars and eagles. Human activity, like logging, is clearing the marmot’s natural habitat and making it easier for predators to reach them.

##### **California condor**

The [California condor](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405) (_Gymnogyps californianus_) is a carnivorous scavenger bird. It feeds on the carcasses of large mammals, like cattle and deer.

California condors are the largest flying birds in North America, with wingspans of [2.75 to 3 meters](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/birds/facts/california-condor) (9 to 10 feet). They are mainly found in the central southern California deserts, but California condors also live in Arizona, Utah, and Mexico.

The IUCN classifies California condors as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405). There are thought to be just [93 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405) in the wild in 2025.

California condors are at risk of lead poisoning from lead bullets in the carcasses they eat. Lead ammunition was [banned in California in 2019](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/birds/facts/california-condor), hopefully reducing the threat to the California condor population over time.

##### **Flattened musk turtle**

The [flattened musk turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/20824/97383753) (_Sternotherus depressus_) gets its name from the shape of its shell, which is flatter than that of most other turtles. Their shells range in color from dark brown to yellow-brown.

These small turtles have shells that measure, at most, [11 centimeters](https://www.outdooralabama.com/turtles/flattened-musk-turtle) (4.3 inches). They are only found in Alabama.

This freshwater turtle prefers to live in free-flowing creeks or small rivers with vegetation in the shallows and lots of rock coverage. They eat mollusks and aquatic insects.

The IUCN lists the flattened musk turtle as [critically endangered with a decreasing population](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/20824/97383753). These turtles are threatened by habitat degradation. Pollution and silt are damaging the waterways where flattened musk turtles live.

##### **Ivory-billed woodpecker**

The [ivory-billed woodpecker](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22681425/182588014) (_Campephilus principalis_) has distinctive black and white colouring and yellow eyes. Male ivory-billed woodpeckers have a red crest, making them easily distinguishable from females.

These birds live in forest and swamp habitats, feeding on deadwood insects. The ivory-billed woodpecker is the [largest woodpecker in the US](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/16/us/ivory-billed-woodpecker-not-extinct-yet-climate/index.html), with an estimated wingspan of [76 to 80 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/ivory-billed-woodpecker-campephilus-principalis) (30 to 31 inches).

Unfortunately, the ivory-billed woodpecker may already [be extinct](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/16/us/ivory-billed-woodpecker-not-extinct-yet-climate/index.html). There has been no concrete evidence of its existence since 1987. These birds prefer to live in undisturbed areas with many trees, but logging and land clearing for farming have impacted their habitat, leading to their decline.

However, some researchers and birdwatchers say they have seen evidence of these birds in recent years. For now, the ivory-billed woodpecker is classed as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22681425/182588014).

##### **Dusky gopher frog**

The [dusky gopher frog](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/58714/118983642#geographic-range) (_Lithobates sevosus_) lives in the forests and wetlands of Mississippi. It’s a black, grey, and brown frog with a warty back and a white-yellow underbelly.

Dusky gopher frogs spend most of their time underground in burrows dug by gopher tortoises and other animals. At night, they venture out to feed on insects and other small animals. In the winter, they travel to temporary ponds to breed.

Male dusky gopher frogs make a loud snoring sound that can be heard [up to half a kilometer (0.3 miles)](https://forestry.alabama.gov/Pages/Informational/Endangered/Dusky_Gopher_Frog.pdf) away. All dusky gopher frogs defend themselves by inflating their bodies and excreting a bitter fluid from the warty glands on their backs.

As of 2025, the IUCN categorises the dusky gopher frog as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/58714/118983642#geographic-range). Dusky gopher frogs live in longleaf pine forests, but [99%](https://www.fs.usda.gov/features/rediscovering-snoring-dusky-gopher-frog-and-restoring-longleaf-pine-forests-rare-species) of America’s longleaf pine forests have been destroyed through land management and urbanisation, the two major threats to this species.

##### **Black-footed ferret**

![Image 5: A wild black-footed ferret stalking prey on the plains of Colorado.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4821/image/p1300x1300/iStock-1183288290_570030_reduced.webp)

A wild black-footed ferret stalking prey on the plains of Colorado. 

The [black-footed ferret](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information) (_Mustela nigripes_) is a carnivorous mammal and [the only ferret species](https://www.fws.gov/species/black-footed-ferret-mustela-nigripes) native to the Americas. They live in shrubland and grassland and have self-sustaining populations in [South Dakota, Wyoming, and Arizona](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#geographic-range).

These animals have light-colored fur with black feet, a black bandit-style facemask, and a black-tipped tail. Their long, slender bodies can measure up to [63 centimeters (25 inches)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/black-footed-ferret) from head to tail.

The black-footed ferret’s main prey is [prairie dogs](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/prairie-dogs). [During the 20th century](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/black-footed-ferret), farmers and ranchers were allowed to kill prairie dogs because of the damage their burrows did to their fields—nearly wiping out the black-footed ferret population in the process.

The IUCN classifies the black-footed ferret as [endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information). Their numbers are decreasing, and, as of 2025, there are thought to be only [206 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information) left in the wild.

##### **Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander**

[Hickory Nut Gorge green salamanders](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) (_Aneides caryaensis_) are named after the only place they live—Hickory Nut Gorge in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina. Here, they nest in the hollows and crevices of rocky outcrops.

This small salamander measures just [55 millimeters](https://auth1.dpr.ncparks.gov/amphibians/view.php?checklist_number=41.0) (2 inches) long. It has a dark brown-black color with patches of bright green-yellow. This coloring acts as camouflage among the moss and lichen of this [22-kilometer](https://gardenandgun.com/articles/meet-the-souths-newest-salamander/) (14-mile) long canyon.

The IUCN categorizes the Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) with just [249 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) remaining in 2025—and their population is decreasing. Habit loss and fragmentation due to tourism and real estate development are the main threats to the Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander.

##### **Bog turtle**

One of the smallest turtle species in the world, [bog turtles](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/4967/97416755) (_Glyptemys muhlenbergii_) measure only [11.5 centimeters (4.5 inches) long](https://www.fws.gov/species/bog-turtle-glyptemys-muhlenbergii). Bog turtles are mostly dark brown but have a bright orange-yellow patch on each side of their head.

These semi-aquatic creatures live in shallow wetland regions. They like areas that aren’t too densely forested, because the plants they like to eat need plenty of sunlight to grow.

There are [two main populations of bog turtles](https://www.fws.gov/species/bog-turtle-glyptemys-muhlenbergii). One population is found throughout Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. The other population lives throughout Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Virginia.

The IUCN classifies the bog turtle as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/4967/97416755), with an unknown number of bog turtles remaining in the wild. Fragmentation of their habitat plus the effect of agriculture on the quality of wetlands are significant threats to the bog turtle.

##### **Houston toad**

![Image 6: A Houston toad in the grass.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4822/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_494484962_570117_reduced.webp)

A Houston toad in the grass. 

The [Houston toad](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321) (_Anaxyrus houstonensis_) measures [just 5 to 9 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/houston-toad-bufo-houstonensis) (2 to 3.5 inches). It has dark brown, speckled coloring and a pale, dark-spotted underbelly.

These toads live exclusively in east to central Texas, mainly in upland pine forests or oak forests with deep, sandy soils.

According to the IUCN, the Houston toad is [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321), with between [85 and 249 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321) left in the wild. The Houston toad population is decreasing.

They’re losing their space to urbanization and road construction, which destroy and fragment habitats, making it harder for toads to move around and breed. Road construction through Houston toad habitats also increases the likelihood of vehicles killing toads. Houston toads also face predation from fire ants that feed on baby toads as they leave their breeding pond.

##### **Laysan duck**

The [Laysan duck](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22680203/130697270) (_Anas laysanensis_) measures up to [43.2 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/laysan-duck-anas-laysanensis) (17 inches) long and weighs up [to 500 grams](https://www.fws.gov/species/laysan-duck-anas-laysanensis) (17.6 ounces). It is primarily chocolate-brown in color with a distinctive white ring around each eye.

It lives on Laysan Island in Hawaii, where it takes shelter in vegetation during the day and comes out to feed at night. The Laysan duck eats insects, larvae, seeds, leaves, and algae.

The Laysan duck is considered [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22680203/130697270) due to several threats. Historically, the introduction of rabbits to Laysan Island led to a loss of vegetation, degrading the Laysan duck’s habitat and causing population decline. Disease and invasive plant species are also affecting the Laysan duck’s survival.

##### **Georgetown salamander**

The [Georgetown salamander](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/59271/118991199) (_Eurycea naufragia_) lives in gravel and under rocks in caves and freshwater springs. It’s found in the San Gabriel River in central Texas.

This salamander was only discovered and described [in 2000](https://amphibiaweb.org/cgi/amphib_query?where-genus=Eurycea&where-species=naufragia&account=lannoo), so we don’t know much about it. However, we do know that they’re very sensitive to water quality and tend to be found near spring outflow.

The IUCN lists the Georgetown salamander as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/59271/118991199). Their numbers are decreasing, and their habitat is being destroyed by development.

##### **Coahuilan box turtle**

The [Coahuilan box turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/21642/97428806) (_Terrapene coahuila_) is an aquatic box turtle that lives in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin of central Coahuila, Mexico. It lives in ponds and wetlands and buries itself in mud to stabilize its body temperature.

Their shells measure up to [16.8 centimeters](https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Terrapene_coahuila/) (around 6.5 inches) in diameter, and adults weigh [an average of 568 grams](https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Terrapene_coahuila/) (20 ounces). The Coahuilan box turtle is an omnivore. It usually eats aquatic insects, algae, and mushrooms, but has also been known to eat spiders, fish, and crustaceans.

The IUCN classifies the Coahuilan box turtle as [endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/21642/97428806). Its numbers are decreasing, and it is threatened by human activity in its habitat, including canal digging and groundwater pumping.

# 20 of the most endangered animals in North America

November 20, 2025

Want to help wildlife?[Join IFAW](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/20-most-endangered-animals-north-america?form=join)

In [Asia](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/18-of-the-most-endangered-animals-in-asia), [South America](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/16-most-endangered-animals-south-america), [Europe](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/most-endangered-species-europe), and beyond, wild animals are threatened by human activity. It’s no different in North America, where [more than one-third of US wildlife](https://www.livescience.com/more-than-a-third-of-us-wildlife-at-risk-of-extinction-grim-new-report-shows) is at risk of extinction.

Every animal—from the largest predator to the smallest insect—plays an essential part in its ecosystem. The loss of just one species has a significant impact on countless others. That’s why, at IFAW, we’re working to protect animals in North America and around the world. From [marine conservation](https://www.ifaw.org/programs/marine-conservation) to [disaster response](https://www.ifaw.org/programs/disaster-response) to raising public awareness of the threats animals face, we’re building a future where animals and people can thrive together.

Here, we look at the 20 most endangered animals in North America and the unique threats that each species faces.

##### **Red wolf**

![Image 1: Red wolf.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4062/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_503024760_441363_reduced.webp)

Red wolf. 

[Red wolves](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population) (_Canis rufus)_ are part of the dog family. They’re smaller than [grey wolves](http://ifaw.org/animals/wolves) but bigger than coyotes. As their name suggests, red wolves have tawny, red-grey coats.

Red wolves used to live throughout the eastern and southern US. They now live solely in North Carolina. They can thrive in various habitats, including forests, swamps, and coastal prairies, where they hunt white-tailed deer, raccoons, rabbits, and other small mammals.

Red wolves were declared extinct in the wild in [1980](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#assessment-information) but were reintroduced to North Carolina in [1987](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#assessment-information). The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) now categorizes red wolves as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population).

As of 2025, their population is still decreasing, with just [20 to 30 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3747/163509841#population) left in the wild.

Red wolves face several threats, including hybridization with coyotes. Illegal killing of red wolves also continues, particularly when wolves come into conflict with landowners.

At IFAW, we’re [campaigning to end the practice of poisoning predators](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/predator-protection-canada) like wolves in Canada. We’re also working with local communities to promote peaceful [coexistence with wolves](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/predator-coexistence-united-states) and the use of non-lethal methods to reduce [human-wildlife conflicts](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/what-is-human-wildlife-conflict).

##### **Axolotl**

The [axolotl](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/1095/53947343) (_Ambystoma mexicanum_) is a unique-looking amphibian creature with feathery gills, webbed feet, a dorsal fin, and a mouth curved upwards into a permanent smile.

Axolotls are salamanders that never grow out of the larval phase. Instead, they continue to live in water and, unlike other amphibians, never make the transition to land.

Axolotls grow to be just [25 centimeters (10 inches)](https://www.britannica.com/animal/axolotl) long. They eat crustaceans, insect eggs, mollusks, and small fish. In the wild, their coloring is mostly grey-brown.

This animal is only found in Lake Xochimilco, a water system made up of canals, small lakes, and wetlands in Mexico City.

In 2025, the IUCN categorizes axolotls as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/1095/53947343), with a decreasing population. Despite improvements in recent years, pollution and draining of their habitat (to reduce flood risk) continue to threaten their survival.

##### **North Atlantic right whale**

![Image 2: North Atlantic right whale Horton (Catalog #3360) and the second calf of the 2023-4 calving season](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4818/image/p1300x1300/MC202312_NARWSecondCalf_002_459613_reduced.webp)

North Atlantic right whale Horton (Catalog #3360) and the second calf of the 2023-4 calving season, sighted December 07, 2023 approximately 22.2mi east of St. Catherine’s Island, GA. Photo: © Clearwater Marine Aquarium Research Institute, taken under NOAA permit #26919. Funded by United States Army Corps of Engineers

[The North Atlantic right whale](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/north-atlantic-right-whale) (_Eubalaena glacialis_) is a huge, slow-swimming baleen whale. It can grow up to [15 meters](https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/species-guide/north-atlantic-right-whale/) (49 feet) long and weigh [70,000 kilograms](https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/species-guide/north-atlantic-right-whale/)(154,000 pounds).

These whales live in the Atlantic Ocean, swimming in deep waters when searching for food and moving to shallower areas when calving. They feed on zooplankton, krill, and other small crustaceans.

The IUCN classes North Atlantic right whales as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/41712/178589687). As of 2025, only around [370 North Atlantic right whales](https://www.ifaw.org/press-releases/north-atlantic-right-whales-number-urgency) are left, with just [70 reproductive-age females](https://www.ifaw.org/campaigns/north-atlantic-right-whale-calving-season).

Key threats to North Atlantic right whales include [vessel strikes](https://www.ifaw.org/resources/ship-strikes-whales-prevention-factsheet) and entanglement in fishing gear. Whales are coming into contact with humans and fishing activity more regularly because climate change has shifted their usual habitats, increasing the danger members of the species face.

At IFAW, we’re working hard to [ensure the survival of the North Atlantic right whale](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/saving-the-north-atlantic-right-whale), by advocating for solutions to their biggest threats, vessel strikes and entanglement. Help us save this species by adding your name to our petition.

[Sign the petition](http://action.ifaw.org/page/125066/action/1)

##### **Bolson tortoise**

The [Bolson tortoise](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985) (_Gopherus flavomarginatus_) is the world’s [largest land reptile](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus). It can grow to [40 centimeters (5.75 inches)](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus), with females growing larger than males. The Bolson tortoise lives in a small area of grassland in Mexico and grazes on grasses and other plants.

This species of tortoise spends most of its time in an underground burrow that it digs with its front feet. These burrows are around [2.5 meters (8 feet) deep](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus) and [10 meters (32 feet) long](https://www.fws.gov/species/bolson-tortoise-gopherus-flavomarginatus) and help protect the tortoises from predators and extreme temperatures.

The IUCN lists the Bolson tortoise as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985). As of 2025, there are around [2,500 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/9402/112660985) left, and their population is decreasing. Habitat degradation and overgrazing by cattle impact the grassland habitat where the Bolson tortoise lives, further threatening this species.

##### **Mojave Desert tortoise**

The [Mojave Desert tortoise](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/97246272/3150871#population) (_Gopherus agassizii_) has survived in the Mojave Desert for [millions of years](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/desert-tortoises). These medium-sized tortoises measure [23 to 28 centimeters](https://www.ifaw.org/au/animals/desert-tortoises) (9 to 15 inches) and weigh [3.5 to 7 kilograms](https://www.ifaw.org/au/animals/desert-tortoises)(8 to 15 pounds) as adults.

Mojave Desert tortoises are herbivores that feed on grasses, wildflowers, herbs, shrubs, and even cacti. They spend much of the year in hibernation, retreating to underground burrows to avoid the extreme temperatures of the desert.

The IUCN lists the Mojave Desert tortoise as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/97246272/3150871#population). Their population is severely fragmented, and adult numbers decreased by[36%](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2024-10/usfws_dtmonitoringupdate_mog_20241003_mitchell.pdf) between 2001 and 2020.

Human activity is largely to blame for the decline of the Mojave Desert tortoise. Towns, cities, and roads are breaking up and encroaching on the tortoise’s desert habitat. Additionally, invasive grasses are outcompeting the native plants that the Mojave Desert tortoise likes to eat, threatening their food sources.

##### **Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle**

![Image 3: After stranding in Cape Cod and undergoing four months of rehabilitation, a Kemp's ridley turtle is returned to the wild in New Smyrna Beach, Florida.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4819/image/p1300x1300/DSC_0063-2_edited.webp)

After stranding in Cape Cod and undergoing four months of rehabilitation, a Kemp's ridley turtle is returned to the wild in New Smyrna Beach, Florida. Photo: © IFAW

[Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/11533/155057916) (_Lepidochelys kempii_) is the world’s smallest sea turtle. Their shells typically measure up to [60 centimeters (2 feet)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle) in diameter and weigh up to [45 kilograms (100 pounds)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle). They can live to be [50 years old](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/kemps-ridley-sea-turtle).

In North America, most of these [sea turtles](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/sea-turtles) live in the Gulf of Mexico, but you can find them as far north as Nova Scotia.

Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles are migratory and can travel hundreds of miles when it’s time to lay their eggs. Females travel to the same beach where they hatched decades ago. There, they participate in a nesting procession called an [arribada](https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/reptiles/kemps-ridley-nesting-arribada). They drag their bodies across the beach in large groups, searching for the perfect place to lay their eggs.

The IUCN lists Kemp’s Ridley sea turtle as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/11533/155057916). The biggest threat to their survival is fishing activity. The turtles get accidentally caught by fishing boats, which can lead to drowning or fatal injuries.

[Sign our petitions to protect animals](https://www.ifaw.org/take-action)

##### **Rice’s whale**

[Rice’s whale](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) (_Balaenoptera ricei_) lives in the Gulf of Mexico. They can grow up to [12.5 meters (41 feet)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) long and weigh up to [27,200 kilograms (60,000 pounds)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale).

These baleen whales dive to the bottom of the sea during the day and spend the night within [15 meters (50 feet)](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) of the surface.

The IUCN lists Rice’s whale as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244). As of 2025, there are only [26 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) left, and their population is decreasing, making this [one of the most endangered whales](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/rices-whale) in the world.

These whales are most at risk from vessel strikes and entanglement in fishing gear. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill affected Rice’s whale habitat, too. Around [48% of the population](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/215823373/208496244) was exposed to oil, causing reproductive failure and ill health.

IFAW is campaigning for [reduced vessel speeds](https://www.ifaw.org/journal/protection-whales-climate-change-ship-speed-reduction), which would decrease the risk of [collisions](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/21st-century-shipping) and reduce [ocean noise pollution](https://www.ifaw.org/projects/ocean-noise-reduction-global). We’re also supporting the development of ropeless [fishing gear](https://www.ifaw.org/people/opinions/new-fishing-gear-crucial-saving-whales) to prevent entanglements.

##### **Hot Creek toad**

The [Hot Creek toad](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/181491536/182617236) (_Anaxyrus monfontanus_) is a toad species that was [only discovered in 2017](https://www.unr.edu/nevada-today/news/2017/new-toad-species-discovered). It has olive-grey coloring and lives in Nevada’s Great Basin in the Hot Creek Mountain Range. This area of marshy habitat is fed by hot springs and surrounded by a high-altitude desert, which may help to explain why these toads are confined to such a small and remote habitat.

Because we haven’t known about the Hot Creek toad for long, we don’t know much about its behavior or what conditions it needs for survival. The number of Hot Creek toads in the wild is also unknown, but the IUCN categorizes the species as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/181491536/182617236).

##### **Vancouver Island marmot**

![Image 4: Two Vancouver Island marmots on a rock.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4065/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_212902763_441366_reduced.webp)

Two Vancouver Island marmots on a rock. 

The [Vancouver Island marmot](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184) (_Marmota vancouverensis_) lives in the forest, grassland, and rocky mountain habitat of Canada’s Vancouver Island.

They are dark brown with white patches on their noses, their bellies, and the tops of their heads. They have brown, bushy tails.

This species is quite large compared to other marmots and rodents. They tend to be around [62 to 72 centimeters](https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/endangered-species/vancouver-island-marmot/) (just over 2 feet) long and weigh [3.5 to 5.5 kilograms](https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/endangered-species/vancouver-island-marmot/) (7-12 pounds). They lose weight during winter hibernation and put it back on in the spring and summer.

The IUCN categorizes the Vancouver Island marmot as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184). As of 2025, there are just [90 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/12828/22259184) left in the wild.

These marmots are particularly at risk from predators like cougars and eagles. Human activity, like logging, is clearing the marmot’s natural habitat and making it easier for predators to reach them.

##### **California condor**

The [California condor](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405) (_Gymnogyps californianus_) is a carnivorous scavenger bird. It feeds on the carcasses of large mammals, like cattle and deer.

California condors are the largest flying birds in North America, with wingspans of [2.75 to 3 meters](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/birds/facts/california-condor) (9 to 10 feet). They are mainly found in the central southern California deserts, but California condors also live in Arizona, Utah, and Mexico.

The IUCN classifies California condors as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405). There are thought to be just [93 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697636/181151405) in the wild in 2025.

California condors are at risk of lead poisoning from lead bullets in the carcasses they eat. Lead ammunition was [banned in California in 2019](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/birds/facts/california-condor), hopefully reducing the threat to the California condor population over time.

##### **Flattened musk turtle**

The [flattened musk turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/20824/97383753) (_Sternotherus depressus_) gets its name from the shape of its shell, which is flatter than that of most other turtles. Their shells range in color from dark brown to yellow-brown.

These small turtles have shells that measure, at most, [11 centimeters](https://www.outdooralabama.com/turtles/flattened-musk-turtle) (4.3 inches). They are only found in Alabama.

This freshwater turtle prefers to live in free-flowing creeks or small rivers with vegetation in the shallows and lots of rock coverage. They eat mollusks and aquatic insects.

The IUCN lists the flattened musk turtle as [critically endangered with a decreasing population](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/20824/97383753). These turtles are threatened by habitat degradation. Pollution and silt are damaging the waterways where flattened musk turtles live.

##### **Ivory-billed woodpecker**

The [ivory-billed woodpecker](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22681425/182588014) (_Campephilus principalis_) has distinctive black and white colouring and yellow eyes. Male ivory-billed woodpeckers have a red crest, making them easily distinguishable from females.

These birds live in forest and swamp habitats, feeding on deadwood insects. The ivory-billed woodpecker is the [largest woodpecker in the US](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/16/us/ivory-billed-woodpecker-not-extinct-yet-climate/index.html), with an estimated wingspan of [76 to 80 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/ivory-billed-woodpecker-campephilus-principalis) (30 to 31 inches).

Unfortunately, the ivory-billed woodpecker may already [be extinct](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/16/us/ivory-billed-woodpecker-not-extinct-yet-climate/index.html). There has been no concrete evidence of its existence since 1987. These birds prefer to live in undisturbed areas with many trees, but logging and land clearing for farming have impacted their habitat, leading to their decline.

However, some researchers and birdwatchers say they have seen evidence of these birds in recent years. For now, the ivory-billed woodpecker is classed as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22681425/182588014).

##### **Dusky gopher frog**

The [dusky gopher frog](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/58714/118983642#geographic-range) (_Lithobates sevosus_) lives in the forests and wetlands of Mississippi. It’s a black, grey, and brown frog with a warty back and a white-yellow underbelly.

Dusky gopher frogs spend most of their time underground in burrows dug by gopher tortoises and other animals. At night, they venture out to feed on insects and other small animals. In the winter, they travel to temporary ponds to breed.

Male dusky gopher frogs make a loud snoring sound that can be heard [up to half a kilometer (0.3 miles)](https://forestry.alabama.gov/Pages/Informational/Endangered/Dusky_Gopher_Frog.pdf) away. All dusky gopher frogs defend themselves by inflating their bodies and excreting a bitter fluid from the warty glands on their backs.

As of 2025, the IUCN categorises the dusky gopher frog as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/58714/118983642#geographic-range). Dusky gopher frogs live in longleaf pine forests, but [99%](https://www.fs.usda.gov/features/rediscovering-snoring-dusky-gopher-frog-and-restoring-longleaf-pine-forests-rare-species) of America’s longleaf pine forests have been destroyed through land management and urbanisation, the two major threats to this species.

##### **Black-footed ferret**

![Image 5: A wild black-footed ferret stalking prey on the plains of Colorado.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4821/image/p1300x1300/iStock-1183288290_570030_reduced.webp)

A wild black-footed ferret stalking prey on the plains of Colorado. 

The [black-footed ferret](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information) (_Mustela nigripes_) is a carnivorous mammal and [the only ferret species](https://www.fws.gov/species/black-footed-ferret-mustela-nigripes) native to the Americas. They live in shrubland and grassland and have self-sustaining populations in [South Dakota, Wyoming, and Arizona](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#geographic-range).

These animals have light-colored fur with black feet, a black bandit-style facemask, and a black-tipped tail. Their long, slender bodies can measure up to [63 centimeters (25 inches)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/black-footed-ferret) from head to tail.

The black-footed ferret’s main prey is [prairie dogs](https://www.ifaw.org/animals/prairie-dogs). [During the 20th century](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/black-footed-ferret), farmers and ranchers were allowed to kill prairie dogs because of the damage their burrows did to their fields—nearly wiping out the black-footed ferret population in the process.

The IUCN classifies the black-footed ferret as [endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information). Their numbers are decreasing, and, as of 2025, there are thought to be only [206 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/14020/45200314#assessment-information) left in the wild.

##### **Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander**

[Hickory Nut Gorge green salamanders](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) (_Aneides caryaensis_) are named after the only place they live—Hickory Nut Gorge in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina. Here, they nest in the hollows and crevices of rocky outcrops.

This small salamander measures just [55 millimeters](https://auth1.dpr.ncparks.gov/amphibians/view.php?checklist_number=41.0) (2 inches) long. It has a dark brown-black color with patches of bright green-yellow. This coloring acts as camouflage among the moss and lichen of this [22-kilometer](https://gardenandgun.com/articles/meet-the-souths-newest-salamander/) (14-mile) long canyon.

The IUCN categorizes the Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) with just [249 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/200106196/200106209) remaining in 2025—and their population is decreasing. Habit loss and fragmentation due to tourism and real estate development are the main threats to the Hickory Nut Gorge green salamander.

##### **Bog turtle**

One of the smallest turtle species in the world, [bog turtles](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/4967/97416755) (_Glyptemys muhlenbergii_) measure only [11.5 centimeters (4.5 inches) long](https://www.fws.gov/species/bog-turtle-glyptemys-muhlenbergii). Bog turtles are mostly dark brown but have a bright orange-yellow patch on each side of their head.

These semi-aquatic creatures live in shallow wetland regions. They like areas that aren’t too densely forested, because the plants they like to eat need plenty of sunlight to grow.

There are [two main populations of bog turtles](https://www.fws.gov/species/bog-turtle-glyptemys-muhlenbergii). One population is found throughout Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. The other population lives throughout Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Virginia.

The IUCN classifies the bog turtle as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/4967/97416755), with an unknown number of bog turtles remaining in the wild. Fragmentation of their habitat plus the effect of agriculture on the quality of wetlands are significant threats to the bog turtle.

##### **Houston toad**

![Image 6: A Houston toad in the grass.](https://d1jyxxz9imt9yb.cloudfront.net/medialib/4822/image/p1300x1300/AdobeStock_494484962_570117_reduced.webp)

A Houston toad in the grass. 

The [Houston toad](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321) (_Anaxyrus houstonensis_) measures [just 5 to 9 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/houston-toad-bufo-houstonensis) (2 to 3.5 inches). It has dark brown, speckled coloring and a pale, dark-spotted underbelly.

These toads live exclusively in east to central Texas, mainly in upland pine forests or oak forests with deep, sandy soils.

According to the IUCN, the Houston toad is [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321), with between [85 and 249 mature individuals](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/3170/118972321) left in the wild. The Houston toad population is decreasing.

They’re losing their space to urbanization and road construction, which destroy and fragment habitats, making it harder for toads to move around and breed. Road construction through Houston toad habitats also increases the likelihood of vehicles killing toads. Houston toads also face predation from fire ants that feed on baby toads as they leave their breeding pond.

##### **Laysan duck**

The [Laysan duck](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22680203/130697270) (_Anas laysanensis_) measures up to [43.2 centimeters](https://www.fws.gov/species/laysan-duck-anas-laysanensis) (17 inches) long and weighs up [to 500 grams](https://www.fws.gov/species/laysan-duck-anas-laysanensis) (17.6 ounces). It is primarily chocolate-brown in color with a distinctive white ring around each eye.

It lives on Laysan Island in Hawaii, where it takes shelter in vegetation during the day and comes out to feed at night. The Laysan duck eats insects, larvae, seeds, leaves, and algae.

The Laysan duck is considered [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22680203/130697270) due to several threats. Historically, the introduction of rabbits to Laysan Island led to a loss of vegetation, degrading the Laysan duck’s habitat and causing population decline. Disease and invasive plant species are also affecting the Laysan duck’s survival.

##### **Georgetown salamander**

The [Georgetown salamander](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/59271/118991199) (_Eurycea naufragia_) lives in gravel and under rocks in caves and freshwater springs. It’s found in the San Gabriel River in central Texas.

This salamander was only discovered and described [in 2000](https://amphibiaweb.org/cgi/amphib_query?where-genus=Eurycea&where-species=naufragia&account=lannoo), so we don’t know much about it. However, we do know that they’re very sensitive to water quality and tend to be found near spring outflow.

The IUCN lists the Georgetown salamander as [critically endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/59271/118991199). Their numbers are decreasing, and their habitat is being destroyed by development.

##### **Coahuilan box turtle**

The [Coahuilan box turtle](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/21642/97428806) (_Terrapene coahuila_) is an aquatic box turtle that lives in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin of central Coahuila, Mexico. It lives in ponds and wetlands and buries itself in mud to stabilize its body temperature.

Their shells measure up to [16.8 centimeters](https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Terrapene_coahuila/) (around 6.5 inches) in diameter, and adults weigh [an average of 568 grams](https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Terrapene_coahuila/) (20 ounces). The Coahuilan box turtle is an omnivore. It usually eats aquatic insects, algae, and mushrooms, but has also been known to eat spiders, fish, and crustaceans.

The IUCN classifies the Coahuilan box turtle as [endangered](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/21642/97428806). Its numbers are decreasing, and it is threatened by human activity in its habitat, including canal digging and groundwater pumping.

## **Help IFAW protect endangered animals in North America**

These animals are just the tip of the iceberg. There are many more species in North America at risk of extinction. To ensure their survival and protect vital ecosystems, we need to do all we can to help them.

IFAW is a rescue and conservation organization committed to building a world where animals and people can thrive together.

# European bison recovering, 31 species declared Extinct – IUCN Red List

**Gland, Switzerland, 10 December 2020 (IUCN)** – The European bison (_Bison bonasus_), Europe’s largest land mammal, has moved from Vulnerable to Near Threatened thanks to continued conservation efforts, according to today’s update of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species™. With this update, 31 species also move into the Extinct category, and all of the world’s freshwater dolphin species are now threatened with extinction.

There are now 128,918 species on the IUCN Red List, of which 35,765 are threatened with extinction.

“The European bison and twenty-five other species recoveries documented in today’s IUCN Red List update demonstrate the power of conservation,” said **Dr Bruno Oberle, IUCN Director General.** “Yet the growing list of Extinct species is a stark reminder that conservation efforts must urgently expand. To tackle global threats such as unsustainable fisheries, land clearing for agriculture, and invasive species, conservation needs to happen around the world and be incorporated into all sectors of the economy.”

“The conservation successes in today’s Red List update provide living proof that the world can set, and meet, ambitious biodiversity targets. They further highlight the need for real, measurable commitments as we formulate and implement the post-2020 global biodiversity framework,” said **Dr Jane Smart, Global Director of IUCN’s Biodiversity Conservation Group**.

### Conservation drives European bison recovery

As a result of long-term conservation management, the wild population of **European bison** (_Bison bonasus_) has grown from around 1,800 in 2003 to over 6,200 in 2019, justifying the move from Vulnerable to **Near Threatened**. The species survived only in captivity in the early 20 th century, and was reintroduced to the wild in the 1950s. The largest subpopulations are now found in Poland, Belarus and Russia. There are currently 47 free-ranging European bison herds. However, herds are largely isolated from one another and confined to non-optimal forest habitats, and only eight of them are large enough to be genetically viable in the long term. The species remains dependent on ongoing conservation measures such as translocations of bison to more optimal open habitats and reduction of human-bison conflicts.

“Historically, European bison were reintroduced mostly to forest habitats, where they don’t find enough food in winter. However, when they move out of the forest into agricultural areas, they often find themselves in conflict with people. To reduce the conflict risk and the bison’s dependence on supplementary feeding, it will be important to create protected areas that include open meadows for them to graze”, said **Dr Rafał Kowalczyk, co-author of the new assessment and member of the IUCN SSC Bison Specialist Group**.

### All of the world’s freshwater dolphins now threatened

With the **tucuxi**(_Sotalia fluviatilis_) moving from Data Deficient to **Endangered,**all of the world’s freshwater dolphin species are now listed as threatened on the IUCN Red List. This small grey dolphin species found in the Amazon river system has been severely depleted by incidental mortality in fishing gear, damming of rivers and pollution. Eliminating the use of gillnets – curtains of fishing net that hang in the water – and reducing the number of dams in tucuxi habitat are priorities to enable numbers to recover. Enforcing the ban on the deliberate killing of tucuxis is also essential.

### Extinctions

The **lost shark**(_Carcharhinus obsoletus_), which was only formally described last year,enters the Red List as **Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).**The species was last recorded in 1934. Its habitat in the South China Sea has been extensively fished for more than a century and remains one of the most overexploited marine regions in the world. As it is unlikely that the species could have persisted under this heavy pressure, the lost shark may already be extinct.

All of the **17 freshwater fish species** endemic to Lake Lanao and its outlet in the Philippines are now Extinct (15 species) or Critically Endangered(Possibly Extinct) (two species). The extinctions were caused by predatory introduced species, compounded by overharvesting and destructive fishing methods.

Three Central American**frog species** have been newly declared**Extinct.**Additionally, twenty-two frog species across Central and South America were listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct). The main driver of these drastic declines is chytridiomycosis disease. Conservation efforts to protect critical habitat are helping populations of several other amphibian species to recover. Among them is the **Oaxaca Treefrog** (_Sarcohyla celata_), which **moved from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened**thanks to actions by local communities in Mexico.

### Plants: proteas and oaks under pressure

The protea family has been comprehensively assessed with this update, revealing that 45% (637 of 1,464 species) of these striking flowering plants that grow mainly across the Southern Hemisphere are Vulnerable, Endangered or Critically Endangered. Many of the species have highly restricted ranges, making them more vulnerable to the spread of invasive alien species, changes to natural fire cycles caused by humans and linked with climate change, and loss of habitat to agriculture. The protea family includes three **Macadamia** species – the same species that produce the farmed macadamia nut crop – which have entered the IUCN Red List as threatened with extinction in the wild. The macadamia nut (_Macadamia integrifolia_) is listed as Vulnerable, while _M. ternifolia_ and _M. tetraphylla_ are listed as Endangered.

**Oak trees** have been comprehensively assessed, revealing that almost one third (31%, 113 of 430 species) are threatened with extinction. Nine Asian oaks enter the IUCN Red List already Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct or Possibly Extinct in the Wild). The highest numbers of threatened species are in China and Mexico, followed by Viet Nam, the United States and Malaysia. Land clearance for agriculture and logging are the most common threats in China, Mexico and Southeast Asia. Invasive alien species and diseases and climate change are the key threats to oaks in the United States.

#### Supporting quotes:

“We are proud to have supported the advances in knowledge reflected in this IUCN Red List update, including the assessments of over 1,400 species in the protea plant family. This has revealed significant threats to these plants on multiple continents, and serves as a baseline for monitoring future changes in their extinction risk. The power of this knowledge is essential for guiding conservation policy and action,” said**Masako Yamato, General Manager, Environmental Affairs Division of Toyota Motor Corporation**.

"In addition to documenting both recoveries and extinctions, this update to the Red List includes several species of heavily traded medicinal plants including Nagchatri (_Trillium govanianum_), and Oshá (_Ligusticum porteri_). As we continue to grapple with a global pandemic, these assessments are a testament both to the importance of monitoring trends in a changing environment, and to the critical role of zoos, aquariums, and botanic gardens who contributed to hundreds of species assessments even while under deep financial strain," said **Clayton Meredith, Species Survival Officer for Plants, ABQ BioPark**.

“Oaks are amongst the most charismatic of trees, and they are also keystone species in the habitats they occupy. More than 2,300 species of bird, mosses, fungi, insects, lichens and mammals are recorded as using native oaks for food and shelter in the UK, and the same will be true for the 113 species of oak now threatened with extinction. The loss of just one of these tree species has catastrophic consequences for hundreds of other species,” said **Paul Smith, Secretary General of BGCI**.

“It’s fantastic that 17 new assessments in this update, of threatened plant species at Ebo Forest, Cameroon, have already helped the Cameroon government reach a decision to cancel the logging concession for this vast forest. Ebo Forest is crucial for biodiversity,” said **Dr Martin Cheek, Senior Research Leader of the Africa team at Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew**. “We teach our students that an IUCN Red List assessment can help change the fate of a species, but this is the quickest example I’ve ever seen, and also the most impactful in terms of area of forest saved,” said **Dr Eimear Nic Lughadha, Senior Research Leader in Conservation Assessment and Analysis at Kew**.

“While it’s reassuring to see conservation efforts working for the European bison, the 35,765 species on the Red List that are threatened with extinction are an indisputable reminder that we must persevere with dramatic conservation goals,”**said Sean T. O’Brien, President and CEO of Nature Serve.**“By working together to utilize data science and technology as a means to influence global policy, we can protect our planet’s precious biodiversity.”

“As a conservationist, the most emotionally impactful news to present is the confirmation of extinction. The causes range from overexploiting to disease, with some threats easier to mitigate than others. The impact of chytrid fungus on amphibian populations has been particularly vexing, challenging conservationists worldwide. There have been successes and recoveries, as noted in the update, and we need to redouble our efforts to address this and other emerging disease threats to biodiversity,” said **Dr Thomas E Lacher, Jr., Texas A&M University**.

“Seeing so many species joining the Extinct category, many of which have only just been discovered, is heart-breaking. The Red List is a vital tool that helps us understand the pressures facing the diversity of life and therefore the conservation responses needed. A healthy natural world is vital to our wellbeing - we now need to see a clear focus placed on the recovery of species and the maintenance of diversity within the new Global Biodiversity Framework,” said **Dr Andrew Terry, Director of Conservation and Policy at ZSL**.
